cards.title: Utility and maximum expected utility
cards.hook: When outcomes are uncertain, a rational agent maximises EXPECTED utility, not the best case.
cards.visual:
RouteOutcomesExpected utility
A (short, risky)80% U = +10, 20% U = −100.8×10 + 0.2×(−10) = 6
B (long, safe)100% U = +77 ← choose
formula: Σₛ′ P(Result(a) = s′ | a, s) U(s′)
example: Robot on a slippery floor: forward = 80% target, 20% slip sideways → weigh both.
cards.memory: Average, don't dream: expected beats best case.
cards.trap: Choosing Route A because +10 is the best outcome ignores the 20% −10.
explain: When an action can lead to several outcomes, judge it by its average result weighted by how likely each outcome is: its expected utility.
Route A: 80% chance of +10, 20% chance of −10 → 0.8×10 + 0.2×(−10) = 6. Route B: always +7. A rational agent picks B, even though A has the better best case.
The Markov assumption keeps things manageable: the next state depends only on the current state (and action), not on the whole history.

tex.t: EU(a \mid s) = \sum_{s'} P(s' \mid s, a)\, U(s'), \qquad a^* = \arg\max_a EU(a \mid s)
where: probability that action a in s leads to s′

cards.title: What an MDP is
cards.visual:
4×3 grid world (columns 1-4, rows 1-3)
+1
▓−1
START
cards.hook: An MDP is the formal model of a sequential decision problem under uncertainty.
example: Up from START: 0.8 up, 0.1 left (bumps wall → stays), 0.1 right.
cards.memory: MDP = States, Actions, Transitions, Rewards (+ γ).
cards.trap: MDP = the PROBLEM model; RL = a LEARNING method used when P or R is unknown.
explain: An MDP describes a world where you make a series of decisions and outcomes are random. It has states, actions, a transition model (probabilities of where each action leads) and rewards.
Grid world: the robot tries to move Up, but only goes up 80% of the time; 10% it slips left and 10% right. Every step costs −0.04 (to encourage hurrying); reaching +1 or −1 ends the episode.
MDP = the problem description. Reinforcement learning = a way to learn good behaviour when you DON'T know the probabilities or rewards in advance.

cards.title: Discounted reward and utility of a policy
cards.visual:
Optimal policy, living reward −0.04 (rows 3→1)
→→→+1
↑▓↑−1
↑←←←
cards.hook: Rewards now are worth more than rewards later.
cards.memory: γ shrinks the future: level k of the search tree is weighted γᵏ.
cards.trap: The first reward gets γ⁰ = 1, not γ.
explain: The return adds up all future rewards, but rewards further in the future are multiplied by γ (between 0 and 1) once per step, so they count less. γ close to 1 = patient agent; γ close to 0 = short-sighted.
A policy π says which action to take in EVERY state. The utility of a state under π is the expected discounted return when you start there and follow π.
The picture: arrows on the grid show the optimal policy when each step costs −0.04: head for +1 and steer around −1.

cards.title: Bellman equation and Q-values
cards.hook: A state's value = best action's expected (reward now + discounted value next).
example: If Q(s,Up) = 7.9 and Q(s,Right) = 6.2 then U(s) = 7.9 and π*(s) = Up.
cards.memory: Bellman = Best action, Expected, Look one step ahead.
cards.trap: Forgetting R inside the brackets, or forgetting to weight by P.
explain: The Bellman equation says: the value of a state = the value of its best action. The value of an action is the average over outcomes of (immediate reward + discounted value of where you land).
Q(s, a) is exactly that action value. Once you know Q, acting optimally is easy: pick the action with the largest Q.
Calculate it like a table: one row per possible next state, compute P × (R + γU′), add the rows. Repeat for each action and take the max.

cards.title: Value iteration vs policy iteration
cards.hook: Two ways to solve the Bellman equations.
cards.visual:
Value iterationPolicy iteration
UpdatesU(s) with max over actionsevaluate fixed π (no max), then improve
Equationsnon-linear (max)evaluation is linear
Stopsδ ≤ ε(1−γ)/γpolicy unchanged
Speedmany cheap sweepsoften fewer iterations
example: n states → n Bellman equations, solved recursively in VI.
cards.memory: VI: Values first, policy at the end. PI: Policy first, refine.
cards.trap: Policy EVALUATION has no max (the action is fixed by π).
explain: Value iteration: start with all utilities 0 and repeatedly apply the Bellman update to every state. Values spread out from the rewards until they stop changing; then read off the best action in each state.

Policy iteration: start with any policy. (1) Evaluate it: compute the utilities if you always follow it (no max, because the action is fixed). (2) Improve it: in each state switch to the action with the best one-step look-ahead. Stop when the policy no longer changes.

tex.t: U_i(s) = \sum_{s'} P(s' \mid s, \pi_i(s))\big[R + \gamma U_i(s')\big], \quad \pi_{i+1}(s) = \arg\max_a \sum_{s'} P(s'|s,a)\big[R + \gamma U_i(s')\big]

cards.title: Reinforcement learning family
cards.hook: When you don't know P or R, learn by trying.
cards.visual:
LearnsNeeds model?Update
Direct utility est.U(s)noaverage reward-to-go at trial end
ADPU(s)learns P from countssolve Bellman (all successors)
TDU(s)notoward observed successor
Q-learningQ(s,a)notoward r + γ max Q(s′,·)
cards.memory: TD = Take one step, Drift toward it.
cards.trap: TD adjusts toward the OBSERVED successor; ADP toward ALL successors weighted by probability.
explain: In RL the agent learns by trial and error. Passive RL: the policy is fixed; just learn how good each state is. Active RL: the agent also chooses actions, balancing exploration (try new things) and exploitation (use what works).
Direct utility estimation: after each trial, compute the total reward from each visited state to the end (reward-to-go) and average them. Simple but slow.
ADP: count transitions to estimate P(s′|s,a), then solve the Bellman equations. TD learning: after every single step, nudge U(s) toward 'reward + γ × U(next state)'.

cards.title: Q-learning
cards.hook: Learn the quality of each action directly, with no model of the world.
formula: Q(s,a) ← Q(s,a) + α[r + γ maxₐ′ Q(s′,a′) − Q(s,a)]
R⁺ if n < Nₑ (be curious) else u (be greedy)
example: Exploratory agent: observe s, choose a (explore/exploit), observe r, s′, update Q, repeat.
cards.memory: Q = Quality; use the MAX of the next state.
cards.trap: Using the average of Q(s′,·) or forgetting γ.
explain: Q-learning learns Q(s,a) directly from experience, with no model of the world (model-free).
After each step (s, a, r, s′): the TD target is r + γ × (best Q in the new state). Move Q(s,a) a fraction α of the way toward that target.
The exploration function keeps the agent curious: actions tried fewer than Nₑ times are treated as if they give the optimistic reward R⁺.

tex.t: f(u, n) = \begin{cases} R^+ & n < N_e \\ u & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}

cards.title: MDP & RL hand calculations (Book 3)
cards.hook: Four calculation patterns cover almost every MDP/RL exam item: Q from utilities, one value-iteration sweep, policy evaluation by equations, and the Q-learning update.
cards.visual:
PatternWorked numbers
Q at (1,1)Up 0.706, Left 0.671, Down 0.660, Right 0.631 → Up
VI at (3,3)0.76 → 0.832 → 0.890 → … 0.918
Policy evaluationU(A) = −1 + U(B); U(B) = 5 + 0.5(−1 + U(A)) → U(B) = 8, U(A) = 7
Q-table A→B→Gep1 Q(B) = 5; ep2 Q(A) = 2.25, Q(B) = 7.5
formula: Q ← Q + α[R + γ max Q′ − Q]
example: For each action list the three landing squares with 0.8 / 0.1 / 0.1 and replace any wall bump by 'stay'.
Value flows backwards from the reward one step per episode (or per iteration).
cards.memory: Table first, numbers second: action | landing square | probability | U.
cards.trap: In value iteration the max makes the equations non-linear; in policy evaluation (fixed policy) they are linear.
explain: Value iteration repeats the Bellman update with a max until nothing changes; policy iteration alternates exact evaluation of a fixed policy (linear equations) with greedy improvement, and stops when the policy is stable.
Q-learning needs no model at all; a deep Q-network replaces the table by a neural network and uses experience replay and a target network for stability.

cheat.title: MDP & RL cheat sheet
rows: Q += α(r + γ max Q′ − Q)
traps: MEU uses expected, not best-case utility.
Slips are perpendicular; walls mean stay put.
Q-learning uses max over next actions.
MDP is the model; RL is the learning method.
